---
title: "A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Osmotic concentration and tonicity

### 1.1

Calculate the osmolarity (mOsm L⁻¹) of each solution. Treat the solutions as
ideal and the salts as fully dissociated.

a. 0.15 mol L⁻¹ glucose
b. 0.15 mol L⁻¹ NaCl
c. 0.10 mol L⁻¹ CaCl₂
d. 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl + 0.10 mol L⁻¹ urea

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 150 mOsm L⁻¹ (glucose does not dissociate).
b. 300 mOsm L⁻¹ (Na⁺ + Cl⁻: 2 particles per formula unit).
c. 300 mOsm L⁻¹ (Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻: 3 particles per formula unit).
d. 300 mOsm L⁻¹ (200 from NaCl + 100 from urea).
:::

### 1.2

An animal's body fluids have an osmolarity of 300 mOsm L⁻¹. For each external
medium, state whether the medium is hyperosmotic, isosmotic or hyposmotic to
the body fluids, and the direction in which water tends to move across a
water-permeable body surface.

a. 10 mOsm L⁻¹ (fresh water)
b. 300 mOsm L⁻¹
c. 1,000 mOsm L⁻¹ (seawater)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Hyposmotic; water tends to enter the animal.
b. Isosmotic; no net osmotic water movement.
c. Hyperosmotic; water tends to leave the animal.
:::

### 1.3

Red blood cells (intracellular osmolarity 300 mOsm L⁻¹) are placed in each
solution. State whether the cells swell, shrink or keep their volume.
The membrane is permeable to urea but effectively impermeable to NaCl.

a. 300 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
b. 150 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
c. 600 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
d. 300 mOsm L⁻¹ urea

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Keep their volume (isotonic).
b. Swell (hypotonic).
c. Shrink (hypertonic).
d. Swell, and eventually burst. Urea enters the cells until its concentration
   is equal on both sides, so it exerts no lasting osmotic effect. The cells'
   own trapped solutes then draw water in. The solution is isosmotic but
   hypotonic.
:::

### 1.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Two solutions with the same osmolarity always have the same effect on cell
   volume.
b. Osmolarity depends on the number of dissolved particles, not on their mass.
c. An osmoconformer keeps every internal ion at the same concentration as
   seawater.
d. A hydrostatic pressure can stop net osmotic water movement before the
   solute concentrations on the two sides become equal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Tonicity depends only on solutes that cannot cross the membrane, so
   isosmotic solutions can differ in tonicity (see 1.3 d).
b. True.
c. False. An osmoconformer matches the *total* osmotic concentration of its
   medium but may still regulate individual ions.
d. True.
:::

## Fish in fresh water and seawater

### 2.1

Complete the table for typical teleost (bony) fishes.

| | Freshwater teleost | Marine teleost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body fluids compared with the medium | | |
| Passive water movement | | |
| Passive salt movement | | |
| Drinking | | |
| Urine volume and concentration | | |
| Direction of active NaCl transport at the gills | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Freshwater teleost | Marine teleost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body fluids compared with the medium | Hyperosmotic | Hyposmotic |
| Passive water movement | Inward (gain) | Outward (loss) |
| Passive salt movement | Outward (loss) | Inward (gain) |
| Drinking | Little or none | Drinks seawater |
| Urine volume and concentration | Large volume, dilute | Small volume, about isosmotic to plasma |
| Direction of active NaCl transport at the gills | Uptake from water into blood | Secretion from blood into water |

Food also supplies ions to the freshwater fish. In the marine fish, the kidney
excretes most of the excess divalent ions (Mg²⁺, SO₄²⁻).
:::

### 2.2

Marine sharks have a body-fluid osmolarity slightly above that of seawater.

a. Which two organic solutes do they retain to raise their osmolarity?
b. In which direction does water tend to move across their gills?
c. Which organ secretes their excess NaCl?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Urea and trimethylamine oxide (TMAO). TMAO counteracts the destabilising
   effect of urea on proteins.
b. Slightly inward, so sharks do not need to drink seawater.
c. The rectal gland.
:::

## Epithelial transport

### 3.1

In a typical transporting epithelial cell:

a. On which membrane, apical or basolateral, is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase located?
b. How many Na⁺ and K⁺ ions does it move per ATP, and in which directions?
c. Why is the pump needed for Na⁺ to enter the cell passively across the
   other membrane?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The basolateral membrane.
b. 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed.
c. By removing Na⁺, the pump keeps intracellular Na⁺ low (and the inside
   negative). This creates an inward electrochemical gradient for Na⁺ across
   the apical membrane, which channels and cotransporters use.
:::

### 3.2

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. The kidney reabsorbs water by active transport of water molecules.
b. Water crosses epithelia through aquaporins and between cells, following an
   osmotic gradient created by solute transport.
c. A list of transporters is enough to predict the direction of net transport
   across an epithelium.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. No pump transports water. Water follows osmotic gradients set up by
   active solute transport.
b. True.
c. False. You also need to know whether each transporter is on the apical or
   basolateral membrane.
:::

## The nephron

### 4.1

Put the structures in the order that filtrate passes through them.

a. collecting duct
b. distal convoluted tubule
c. Bowman's capsule
d. thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
e. proximal convoluted tubule
f. descending limb of the loop of Henle
g. renal pelvis

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

c → e → f → d → b → a → g.
:::

### 4.2

Match each nephron segment (1–5) with its main transport function (A–E).

| | Segment |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Proximal convoluted tubule |
| 2 | Descending limb of the loop of Henle |
| 3 | Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle |
| 4 | Distal convoluted tubule |
| 5 | Collecting duct |

| | Function |
| --- | --- |
| A | Reabsorbs NaCl (Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter) but is impermeable to water, so the tubular fluid becomes dilute |
| B | Water reabsorption regulated by ADH; Na⁺ reabsorption regulated by aldosterone |
| C | Reabsorbs about two thirds of the filtered Na⁺ and water, and nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids |
| D | Permeable to water but has low permeability to NaCl; water leaves into the hyperosmotic medulla |
| E | Fine-tunes reabsorption of NaCl and Ca²⁺; its fluid is still hyposmotic to plasma |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1–C, 2–D, 3–A, 4–E, 5–B.
:::

### 4.3

Define *filtration*, *reabsorption*, *secretion* and *excretion* in the kidney,
stating the direction of movement for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Filtration:** bulk flow of plasma water and small solutes from the
  glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.
- **Reabsorption:** movement of a substance from the tubular fluid back into
  the blood.
- **Secretion:** movement of a substance from the blood (via the interstitial
  fluid) into the tubular fluid.
- **Excretion:** the amount of a substance that leaves the body in the urine.
:::

### 4.4

Name the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier, and state which
plasma components are normally almost absent from the filtrate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. Fenestrated capillary endothelium.
2. Glomerular basement membrane.
3. Filtration slits between the foot processes of podocytes.

Blood cells and large plasma proteins such as albumin are almost absent from
the filtrate.
:::

## Renal calculations

### 5.1

For a freely filtered solute, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is
0.10 L min⁻¹ and the plasma concentration is 5 mmol L⁻¹. Reabsorption is
0.40 mmol min⁻¹ and secretion is 0.02 mmol min⁻¹. Urine flow is
0.002 L min⁻¹.

a. Calculate the filtered load.
b. Calculate the excretion rate.
c. Calculate the urine concentration of the solute.
d. Urine flow is halved while the excretion rate stays the same. What is the
   new urine concentration?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration = 0.10 L min⁻¹ × 5 mmol L⁻¹
   = 0.50 mmol min⁻¹.
b. Excretion = 0.50 − 0.40 + 0.02 = 0.12 mmol min⁻¹.
c. Urine concentration = excretion ÷ urine flow = 0.12 ÷ 0.002
   = 60 mmol L⁻¹.
d. 0.12 ÷ 0.001 = 120 mmol L⁻¹. The concentration doubles although the amount
   excreted per minute is unchanged.
:::

### 5.2

The renal clearance of a substance is $C = U \times V / P$, where $U$ is its
urine concentration, $V$ the urine flow and $P$ its plasma concentration.
Inulin is infused into a subject. Plasma inulin is 0.20 mg mL⁻¹, urine inulin
is 25 mg mL⁻¹ and urine flow is 1.0 mL min⁻¹.

a. Calculate the inulin clearance.
b. Why does inulin clearance equal the GFR?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. $C = 25 \times 1.0 / 0.20 = 125$ mL min⁻¹.
b. Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed, secreted nor
   metabolised by the tubule. All filtered inulin is therefore excreted, and
   the volume of plasma cleared per minute equals the volume filtered per
   minute.
:::

### 5.3

The GFR is 125 mL min⁻¹. Four freely filtered substances have the clearances
below. For each, state whether the tubule shows net reabsorption, net
secretion or neither.

a. Glucose: 0 mL min⁻¹
b. Urea: 60 mL min⁻¹
c. Substance X: 125 mL min⁻¹
d. Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH): 600 mL min⁻¹

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Net reabsorption (complete).
b. Net reabsorption (partial).
c. Neither, like inulin.
d. Net secretion.

Clearance below the GFR means net reabsorption; clearance above the GFR means
net secretion.
:::

### 5.4

A person has a GFR of 125 mL min⁻¹ and a plasma glucose concentration of
5 mmol L⁻¹.

a. Calculate the filtered load of glucose in mmol min⁻¹.
b. The maximum rate of tubular glucose reabsorption (transport maximum, $T_m$)
   is 2.0 mmol min⁻¹. How much glucose is excreted at this plasma
   concentration?
c. In uncontrolled diabetes, plasma glucose rises to 20 mmol L⁻¹. Calculate
   the glucose excretion rate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 0.125 L min⁻¹ × 5 mmol L⁻¹ = 0.625 mmol min⁻¹.
b. None. The filtered load is below $T_m$, so all of it is reabsorbed.
c. Filtered load = 0.125 × 20 = 2.5 mmol min⁻¹. Excretion = 2.5 − 2.0 =
   0.5 mmol min⁻¹.
:::

### 5.5

A human kidney filters 180 L of plasma per day and produces 1.5 L of urine per
day. What percentage of the filtered water is reabsorbed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

(180 − 1.5) / 180 × 100 = 99.2 %.
:::

## Concentrating the urine

### 6.1

Put the steps in order for the response to dehydration.

a. Aquaporin-2 water channels are inserted into the apical membrane of
   collecting-duct cells.
b. Plasma osmolarity rises.
c. ADH binds to V2 receptors on collecting-duct cells.
d. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change.
e. Water moves from the collecting duct into the hyperosmotic medullary
   interstitium, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
f. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
g. Plasma osmolarity falls and ADH release decreases.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → f → c → a → e → g. Step g is the negative feedback.
:::

### 6.2

A person must excrete 600 mOsm of solute per day. The maximum urine
osmolarity in humans is about 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹.

a. What is the minimum daily urine volume?
b. A person who lacks ADH (diabetes insipidus) produces urine of
   100 mOsm L⁻¹. What is their daily urine volume for the same solute load?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 600 mOsm ÷ 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹ = 0.5 L day⁻¹.
b. 600 mOsm ÷ 100 mOsm L⁻¹ = 6 L day⁻¹.
:::

### 6.3

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Tubular fluid leaving the thick ascending limb is hyposmotic to plasma.
b. ADH increases urine concentration mainly by reducing the GFR.
c. Without ADH, the collecting duct has low water permeability and the urine
   stays dilute.
d. Urea contributes to the osmotic gradient of the inner medulla.
e. Desert rodents that produce very concentrated urine tend to have
   relatively long loops of Henle.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. True (about 100 mOsm L⁻¹), because NaCl is removed without water.
b. False. ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct, so more
   water is reabsorbed into the medulla.
c. True.
d. True.
e. True. A longer loop (and a thicker medulla) builds a larger
   corticomedullary gradient.
:::

## Nitrogenous waste

### 7.1

Complete the table.

| | Ammonia | Urea | Uric acid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Toxicity | | | |
| Solubility in water | | | |
| Water needed to excrete it | | | |
| Energy cost of synthesis | | | |
| Example animal group | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Ammonia | Urea | Uric acid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Toxicity | High | Low | Very low |
| Solubility in water | High | High | Very low |
| Water needed to excrete it | Large amounts | Moderate | Very little (excreted as a paste) |
| Energy cost of synthesis | None | Moderate | High |
| Example animal group | Teleost fishes, most aquatic invertebrates | Mammals, adult amphibians, sharks | Birds, most reptiles, insects |
:::

### 7.2

Classify each animal as ammonotelic, ureotelic or uricotelic.

a. goldfish
b. human
c. chicken
d. tadpole
e. adult frog
f. desert locust

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Ammonotelic. b. Ureotelic. c. Uricotelic. d. Ammonotelic.
e. Ureotelic. f. Uricotelic.
:::

### 7.3

Why is uric acid, rather than urea, the nitrogenous waste of embryos that
develop inside a shelled (cleidoic) egg?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The egg is a closed system: wastes cannot leave it. Uric acid is insoluble, so
it precipitates and is stored in solid form, where it is neither toxic nor
osmotically active. Urea would stay dissolved and accumulate to toxic
concentrations.
:::

### 7.4

Put the steps of urine formation in an insect in order.

a. Water, ions and useful solutes are reabsorbed in the rectum.
b. K⁺ is actively secreted into the lumen of the Malpighian tubules.
c. Dry waste, including precipitated uric acid, is eliminated with the faeces.
d. Water and solutes, including uric acid, follow into the tubule lumen.
e. The tubule fluid empties into the hindgut.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → e → a → c. The Malpighian tubules produce a fluid isosmotic to the
haemolymph by secretion, not by filtration; the hindgut recovers water.
:::
